answers.answer: Distributed data copies are values held on different network-connected computers, such as the two servers holding the same value in the lesson. CAP says that when a network split prevents communication, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and successful completion of every valid request to a working server. Picking any two letters at all times is misleading: outside partitions CAP does not force a consistency/availability choice, and partition tolerance accounts for communication failures rather than eliminating them. A partition prevents parts from exchanging messages; it is not every node crashing. Both sides can remain running and reachable by clients. Ignoring partitions does not restore a broken connection or deliver changes, so it cannot prevent this failure in a distributed deployment.

evidence.quote: Uses computers that communicate over a network.
When a network split prevents communication, a system cannot guarantee both the latest data and successful completion of every request.
Prevents parts of a system from exchanging messages. Servers on both sides can still be running and receiving requests.
Means the design accounts for these communication failures. It does not promise that every operation remains available.
Adding more servers does not remove this problem. They still need a working connection to share changes.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability.

answers.answer: With no intervening write, a read begun after a write completes must reflect that write. CAP consistency is linearizability: one valid operation order respecting real-time completed-before-started relationships. Overlapping operations may go in either order if valid for one copy; synchronized timestamps are not required. Eventual convergence permits temporarily old copies, while ACID consistency preserves defined database rules. CAP availability requires every valid request reaching a working server eventually to produce a successful result, including data for a read. It has no instantaneous-completion or specified latency requirement. Refusal, an error, or indefinite waiting gives up this per-request guarantee; avoiding stale data that way does not preserve both properties. An uptime percentage measures something different from successful eventual completion of every such request.

evidence.quote: If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write. Returning an older local copy cannot satisfy this guarantee.

Overlapping operations may be placed in either order, provided the resulting order is valid for one copy. The required order follows completed-before-started relationships, not a globally synchronized timestamp on every request.
This differs from eventual convergence and from ACID consistency, which concerns preserving defined database rules.
Means every valid request that reaches a working server eventually gets a successful result.
For a read, that means returning data. Returning 'service unavailable' does not satisfy this guarantee.
CAP availability does not mean fast, immediately answered, or a particular uptime percentage. The theorem requires eventual per-request completion and sets no practical response-time target.

answers.answer: B knows its original value 0 and cannot learn the completed update from A through the broken connection. Because the write of 1 completed before the read and there were no other writes, consistency requires the read to return 1. Returning 0 completes the read but violates consistency. Refusing or waiting indefinitely avoids an incorrect result but violates availability. Guessing 1 happens to match this case, but B lacks evidence distinguishing it from other possible unseen writes, so guessing cannot guarantee correctness and availability across those cases.

evidence.quote: If a write completes before a read begins, and no intervening write changes the value, the read must reflect that write. Returning an older local copy cannot satisfy this guarantee.
B cannot know about a change that no message can deliver.
The read succeeds, but breaks consistency.
B avoids returning old data, but cannot guarantee availability.
Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes. The obstacle is missing information, not a particular database product.

answers.answer: To preserve consistency, continue only safely coordinated operations that can obey the required single order; unsafe reads or writes wait or fail. This need not stop all nodes or operations: in the lesson's three-server majority protocol, a connected pair can commit writes while the isolated server cannot. To preserve availability, separated live nodes keep completing requests using their local information, giving up the guarantee that reads reflect completed writes. A stale read returns an older value; conflicting accepted writes are different changes to the same item made on different sides. Recovery requires exchanging changes and applying a merge, selection, or human-resolution rule. Availability provides neither an automatically safe merge nor a guarantee that every update's intent survives; cross-record business rules need separate protection.

evidence.quote: Preserves consistency during a partition. Some requests must wait or fail.
If the network splits into two servers and one, the connected pair can continue committing writes. The isolated server cannot commit writes on its own.
Safely coordinated operations can continue; favoring consistency need not shut down every part of the system.
Keeps accepting requests during a partition. Each side works with the information it has.
Reads can return older data. If both sides accept writes, they can produce conflicting changes to the same item.
After communication returns, the system exchanges changes. It needs a rule to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve the conflict.
Availability supplies no automatic safe merge. Selecting one conflicting value can lose another user's intent, and cross-record rules require their own protection.

answers.answer: Eventual consistency means copies converge when new updates stop, communication resumes, and all required updates and reconciliation reach every copy. It gives no fixed deadline, immediate read-your-writes guarantee, or assurance that every concurrent edit's intent survives; reconciliation policy determines which resulting state wins or how edits merge. An operation that must never return data older than a completed write should continue only where it can safely preserve consistency during a split; affected clients may wait or fail. After recovery, reads must still obey the completed-write rule before returning successfully. The lesson does not specify a recovery algorithm for this case. An operation permitting temporary old values can keep answering on reachable nodes, exposing staleness and potentially accepting conflicting writes. After recovery it exchanges changes and converges under a chosen merge, selection, or human-resolution policy, whose losses and user effects must be considered. Choose guarantees per operation and its supported read configuration: a database can offer different read guarantees, so a permanent vendor-wide label does not establish every request's behavior. The lesson supplies no vendor-specific configuration procedure. CAP alone does not determine normal-operation latency, capacity, or cost.

evidence.quote: Copies converge if new updates stop, communication resumes and the required updates and reconciliation reach every copy.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state. It does not promise that every conflicting edit survives; the conflict-resolution policy determines the result.
Eventually gives no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee. Applications must decide whether temporary older reads are acceptable.
Preserves consistency during a partition. Some requests must wait or fail.
Once a write completes, later reads must reflect it or a newer write.
After communication returns, the system exchanges changes. It needs a rule to merge them, select one, or ask someone to resolve the conflict.
A database can offer different read guarantees. Choose for the operation rather than assuming every request has the same behavior.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability. It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.
